title: Cellulitis and Erysipelas: Outpatient versus Intravenous Antibiotic Criteria

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with skin and soft tissue infection (purulent: furuncle, carbuncle, abscess; non-purulent: cellulitis, erysipelas, necrotising infection) and animal or human bite wounds: severity, oral versus intravenous choice, MRSA cover, drainage, hospital referral, using the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) protocol with NICE NG141 for penicillin allergy, pregnancy, children and referral triggers. Diabetic foot infection is excluded.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The MOH protocol has no page numbers in the extracted text, so sections are cited; it gives no investigations, admission criteria, penicillin-allergy alternatives, renal dose adjustment, contraindications, monitoring or drainage technique.
The MOH protocol lists piperacillin-tazobactam as 3.375 mg, which is a typographical error for 3.375 g; 3.375 g every 6 hours is shown and must be verified against the original PDF.

The MOH protocol prints vancomycin as 15 mg/kg every 8 hours for purulent infection and every 12 hours for severe non-purulent infection; both are shown as printed and should be checked against the MOH vancomycin therapeutic drug monitoring protocol.

NICE NG141 alternatives for penicillin allergy, pregnancy, children and hospital referral triggers are shown with the NICE source named and are not Saudi MOH recommendations; the MOH protocol does not state them.
Severe pathway for necrotising infection and surgical debridement is not detailed in either source beyond adding clindamycin and hospital referral.
Paediatric MOH doses are not given; children's doses are the NICE NG141 doses and children's vancomycin, teicoplanin and linezolid doses were not read.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: The MOH protocol splits infections into purulent (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess) and non-purulent (cellulitis, erysipelas, necrotising infection); incision and drainage is indicated in all purulent cases. Severity: mild has no systemic signs; moderate has temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, heart rate above 90 beats per minute or comorbidities; severe includes immunocompromise, organ dysfunction or septic shock, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, signs of deeper infection, or failure to improve after drainage and oral antibiotics. Likely pathogens are Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in purulent disease or when MRSA risk factors exist. NICE advises oral antibiotics first unless the person cannot take them or needs intravenous treatment, and review of intravenous therapy by 48 hours.

symptoms: Spreading skin redness, swelling, warmth and pain.
physicalSigns: Temperature above 38 degrees Celsius or heart rate above 90 beats per minute (moderate).
redFlags: Septic shock, organ dysfunction or systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
Immunocompromise or clinical signs of deeper infection (possible necrotising infection, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis): refer to hospital; add clindamycin if necrotising infection.

Infection near the eyes or nose (orbital cellulitis risk), lymphangitis, spreading infection despite oral antibiotics, or inability to take oral antibiotics: consider hospital referral or specialist advice (NICE NG141).
Non-purulent infection with penetrating trauma, MRSA elsewhere with nasal colonisation, or injection drug use.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Signs of deeper infection or organ dysfunction; severe pathway with vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam and clindamycin, and hospital referral.
Collection needing incision and drainage; antibiotics added by severity.

clinicalManagement.title: First minutes
actions: Check temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, mental state: septic shock, organ dysfunction or systemic inflammatory response syndrome means the severe pathway and hospital care.
Classify as purulent or non-purulent and grade severity (mild, moderate, severe).
Mark the edge of the redness and record the time.

clinicalManagement.title: Purulent infection (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess)
actions: Incision and drainage in all cases; send pus for culture.

Mild: drainage only. Moderate (7 to 10 days): clindamycin 600 to 900 mg IV every 8 hours, or doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength (160/800 mg) orally every 12 hours.
Severe (10 to 14 days): vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV every 8 hours, or linezolid 600 mg IV every 12 hours.

Definitive therapy by culture: MRSA - clindamycin, doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, vancomycin or linezolid at the doses above; methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus - flucloxacillin 1 to 2 g IV every 4 to 6 hours, cloxacillin 1 to 2 g IV every 6 hours, cefazolin 1 to 2 g IV every 8 hours or clindamycin 600 to 900 mg IV every 8 hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Non-purulent infection (cellulitis, erysipelas)
actions: Mild, outpatient (5 days): cephalexin 500 mg orally every 6 hours, or doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours, or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 1 g orally every 12 hours.
Moderate, inpatient (7 to 10 days): ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours, or cefazolin 1 to 2 g IV every 8 hours, or clindamycin 600 to 900 mg IV every 8 hours.
Severe (7 to 10 days): vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours plus piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g IV every 6 hours (MOH prints 3.375 mg; verify); add clindamycin if necrotising infection.

clinicalManagement.title: Penicillin allergy, pregnancy, children, face or nose (NICE NG141 fill-ins)
actions: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 5 to 7 days; pregnancy: erythromycin 500 mg four times daily.

Infection near the eyes or nose: co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg orally three times daily for 7 days (clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily plus metronidazole 400 mg three times daily if penicillin-allergic); refer.
Children: use NICE NG141 weight-based doses and seek paediatric advice.

clinicalManagement.title: Animal and human bite wounds
actions: Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 1 g orally every 12 hours, or doxycycline 100 to 200 mg orally every 12 hours, or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally every 12 hours plus metronidazole 250 to 500 mg orally every 8 hours.
Give tetanus toxoid if not vaccinated in the previous 10 years.

clinicalManagement.title: Review and escalate
actions: Reassess if worsening rapidly or no improvement in 2 to 3 days; review intravenous therapy by 48 hours with a view to oral switch.
A course of up to 14 days may be needed after clinical assessment (NICE NG141).

medicationPlan.note: Adult doses are from the MOH protocol; penicillin-allergy, pregnancy and paediatric alternatives are from NICE NG141 and are labelled. Renal dose adjustment is not stated in the MOH protocol; check the MOH formulary and the pharmacy renal dosing guide before giving to a patient with reduced kidney function. The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: No systemic signs: incision and drainage only.
Temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, heart rate above 90 beats per minute, or comorbidities.
Immunocompromise, organ dysfunction or septic shock, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, deeper infection, or no improvement after drainage plus oral antibiotics.
Symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, or do not improve within 2 to 3 days (NICE NG141).

teaching.scope: Adult with skin and soft tissue infection (purulent: furuncle, carbuncle, abscess; non-purulent: cellulitis, erysipelas, necrotising infection) and animal or human bite wounds: severity, oral versus intravenous choice, MRSA cover, drainage, hospital referral, using the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) protocol with NICE NG141 for penicillin allergy, pregnancy, children and referral triggers. Diabetic foot infection is excluded.
learningObjectives: Classify purulent versus non-purulent and grade severity.
Drain purulent collections and choose the antibiotic by severity and MRSA risk.
pitfalls: Antibiotics without drainage for an abscess.
Giving penicillins to a penicillin-allergic patient.
keyPoints: Incision and drainage in all purulent cases.
Severe non-purulent: vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam; add clindamycin if necrotising.
Review intravenous antibiotics by 48 hours and reassess at 2 to 3 days.

lifestyleAndDiet: Elevate the affected limb; treat tinea or skin breaks that allow entry.
